requirements.exclusion: A response to a notification carries no correlating ID, so it is indistinguishable on the wire from any other unsolicited response; unsolicited responses are flagged by base.result-id-matches and base.error-id-matches under BASE-004/BASE-009.
The umbrella clause the BASE and LIFE areas mechanize requirement-by-requirement; it has no observable beyond its constituents.
Dialect support is validation behavior inside each implementation; a trace shows schemas exchanged, not how the receiver processed them.
Whether validation happened, and against which dialect, is implementation-internal; validation outcomes need ground truth about inputs that a trace does not carry.
Judging graceful handling requires knowing the receiver's supported-dialect set, which is not in the trace.
Documentation lives outside the protocol session entirely.
What an implementation assumes is internal; only conduct that follows from an assumption could surface, and attributing it requires the assumption.
Whether a syntactically valid prefix is reverse-DNS for its author cannot be decided without knowing the author's domain.
Icon rendering support is client-internal capability with no wire footprint; the conditional premise (that the client renders icons) is equally invisible.
The umbrella for consumer-side icon hygiene (fetch policy, size limits, origin checks) — all consumer-internal conduct after the recorded session ends.
Rejection is client-side handling after receipt; the trace records the icon metadata served, not what the client did with it.

Restates BASE-013's dialect floor and BASE-016's documentation SHOULD as the section's third numbered rule, unconditionally where BASE-013 scopes itself to schemas without an explicit `$schema` (the same restatement shape as TRAN-049 to TRAN-024). Excluded for BASE-013's reason: dialect support is validation behavior inside each implementation, and a trace shows the schemas exchanged, not how the receiver processed them.

Credential retrieval from the environment is process-local conduct with no wire footprint, and the HTTP half defers to the authorization specification, whose clauses are entered on its own page: AUTH-001 and AUTH-002 restate this sentence there, and the challenge clauses a recording can judge carry checks. One entry for the sentence's SHOULD and SHOULD NOT, as BASE-068 enters it at 2026-07-28.
Extends BASE-022's client-internal rendering-support premise: neither the support nor its absence reaches the wire, and the premise itself (that the client renders icons) is equally invisible.

After negotiation, neither stdio nor HTTP message payloads carry a per-message protocol version, so respect is not observable in message traffic. The one wire artifact — the HTTP `MCP-Protocol-Version` header — is judged under TRAN-017 and TRAN-018.
The client's supported-version set is internal state with no wire footprint; the trace shows the version sent, not the versions available.
The server's supported-version set is internal state with no wire footprint; the trace shows the version answered, not the versions available.

Whether the client supports the answered version is client-internal; a continued session is only evidence of support if the premise is known. TRAN-018 warns on the adjacent observable (a mismatched MCP-Protocol-Version header).
Stdin closure, signals, and process exit are host-OS actions outside the trace event vocabulary (transport-open/close/abort record that a transport ended, not who ended it or how).

Binds an SDK's programming interface — what its callers can configure — which has no protocol representation at all.

Preparedness is a property of the implementation, not of any session it took part in: a trace that happens to contain a version mismatch shows one case handled, and a trace without one evidences nothing. Where the handling has a wire form it is judged under the clause that states it, such as the version negotiation rules.

Framing is enforced at capture time: the JSON Lines trace format cannot represent an embedded-newline violation, so a parseable trace is evidence the rule held. Violations surface as capture-time parse failures, not as trace findings.

Judging Origin validation requires the server's configured allowlist, which recorded traces do not carry. Enforced instead as default-on policy in mcp-everything-server and exercised by its transport integration tests (roadmap M2).

A violation cannot be judged from a trace: trace documents are UTF-8 by construction, so recorded messages prove nothing was mis-encoded among what was recorded — and absence is not evidence, because capture tooling may drop undecodable bytes (mcp-everything-server's tap skips non-UTF-8 SSE chunks and unparseable POST bodies). No offline check is sound.

Recorded HTTP events carry status and conformance-relevant headers, not request lines, so endpoint topology is invisible in a trace. Enforced by mcp-everything-server's transport integration tests (roadmap M2).

Judging whether an Origin value is invalid requires the server's configured allowlist, which recorded traces do not carry (the TRAN-002 rationale). Enforced as default-on policy in mcp-everything-server with 403 tests (roadmap M2).

Socket binding is deployment state with no trace footprint. mcp-everything-server defaults to a loopback bind (the --bind clap default in src/main.rs), asserted by default_bind_is_loopback in tests/cli.rs.

Whether authentication is properly implemented is not decidable from one session's headers: the client's credential is never recorded, and the server's validation of it is internal. What a recording does show — the challenge a protected server answers with — is judged under the authorization page's own clauses (AUTH-014, AUTH-045, AUTH-049–AUTH-051).

Global uniqueness and entropy of an identifier cannot be established from the single sample a trace contains. mcp-everything-server's ids are pinned to the v4-UUID shape (OS RNG) and distinctness by session_ids_are_version_4_uuids_and_distinct in tests/http_policy.rs.
Secure handling (storage, exposure, logging discipline) is client-internal behavior with no wire footprint beyond the echo requirement judged under TRAN-013.
Whether a server requires a session ID is server configuration a trace does not carry; without it, a non-400 answer to a session-less request is not evidence either way.
Session termination is server-internal state; a trace cannot distinguish a terminated session (404 required) from a live one (404 forbidden).

A 404 is attributed to the request it answered when the recording's order is unambiguous, but not to the moment the client read it: a recorder logs the status as it passes, and the client may already have sent further requests on the old session. Requests after the 404 therefore do not show the client ignored it, and a client that stops instead of reconnecting sends nothing to judge.
Which version a server assumed is internal state; subsequent traffic does not reveal it.
How a client interprets stderr is internal, and stderr bytes are not part of the protocol trace (the trace records MCP messages and transport lifecycle, not diagnostics channels).
A client's supported-transport surface is a property of the implementation, not of any one session; a streamable-HTTP trace says nothing about whether stdio was available.
The trace vocabulary covers stdio and streamable HTTP; custom transports are outside the capture universe by construction (TransportKind is closed per revision).

Adds to TRAN-049's verb obligation that each message ride a *new* POST to the MCP endpoint. A POST body is one JSON value, which a recorder writes as one payload, so more than one message in a POST is a batch array — TRAN-026 judges that. What remains — that the request was new rather than reused, and was addressed to the MCP endpoint — leaves no trace: the endpoint is not recorded.

Whether input was acceptable is server-internal judgment, and the trace schema records HTTP request and response observations as independent events without request/response correlation, so which response answered which POST is not decidable offline; the official suite exercises this live and the conformance gate runs it.
What a client could have handled is client-internal capability; a trace shows the case that occurred, not the cases supported.

Conditional on client intent (the wish to resume): a session that never disconnects owes nothing, and a recording cannot show a client wishing. When a resumption does occur its method and `last-event-id` header are both recorded, but absence proves nothing.
Which HTTP stream delivered a message is not part of the trace vocabulary — events form a single capture-ordered sequence — so per-stream conduct cannot be judged from a recorded trace.

Conditional on client intent (no longer needing the session). A teardown DELETE is recorded when it happens — `corpus/good/http-session.jsonl` carries one — but a session that ends without one may simply not have finished with it, so absence is not a violation.

The obligation arises when the server closes the connection without terminating the SSE stream, and that is connection- and SSE-frame-level conduct the capture consumes (TRAN-032's reason), so no trace shows when it arose. A later reconnecting `GET` is equally consistent with any other reason to open one, as for TRAN-046.

Binds a transport's documentation, not its messages: the artefact the clause asks for is a document, and no session can be evidence about whether one exists. Custom transports are outside the capture universe besides (TRAN-023).

"Periodically" is a rate over wall-clock time, and checks may not consult time — the limit LIFE-015 records. A recording would have to show the interval between pings against the length of the session, and it carries neither: a session with no ping and one with few are both what a conforming implementation produces over a short enough connection.

Binds the implementation's configuration surface — what its operator can set — which has no protocol representation (LIFE-019's boundary). A recording shows the pings one configuration produced, never whether another was available.

A timeout is a duration held inside the sender, and checks may not consult time (LIFE-015). A recording would have to carry the deadline the sender held a ping to and the network it was chosen for; it shows a ping answered or not, and nothing of either.

"Excessive" is a rate — pings per unit of time — and checks may not consult time (LIFE-015). No count of pings alone separates a flood from a long session checking its connection, the same limit PROG-018 records for rate limiting.

The antecedent, a ping timing out, is the sender's own deadline expiring, which no message records and checks may not compute from timestamps (LIFE-015). The consequence, treating the connection as failed, is at most a `transport-close` lifecycle event, which says that a transport ended and not why; a recording cannot tell a connection dropped for a timeout from one closed at the end of a session.
Logging is local diagnostics with no wire footprint (CANC-024's boundary): nothing an implementation writes to its own log is a protocol message, so no recording contains it.

Whether a message is relevant and human readable is a judgment about its meaning, not its shape; any string satisfies the schema, and no mechanical reading of one decides relevance. The same sentence is PROG-004 at 2026-07-28, excluded for the same reason.

Tracking is bookkeeping inside each party, and a recording carries no message that shows a token being tracked or forgotten. Its wire consequences are the MUST rows beside it, which are judged: a token reused while its request is active (PROG-010), a token no request provided and progress for a finished request (PROG-013, PROG-016, PROG-019).
A rate is messages per unit of time, and checks may not consult time — the limit LIFE-015 records. No count of notifications alone separates a flood from a long operation reporting often.

Ignoring a response is the absence of a reaction inside the sender. A recording would have to carry a message the sender sends because it acted on the late response, and the protocol defines none: nothing a party does with a response it received reaches the wire.

Graceful handling is internal; the race itself is what a recording shows, and the checks are built not to convict it — `cancellation.no-response-after-cancellation` reports an answer to a cancelled request only once the receiver has demonstrably read the cancellation, and the conforming `stdio-cancellation` trace pins the answer that crosses one. A recording would have to carry a message the specification defines as ungraceful handling, and it defines none; a party that failed to handle the race would show it through some other clause's violation, judged there.
Logging is local diagnostics with no wire footprint: nothing an implementation writes to its own log is a protocol message, so no recording contains it.
User-interface presentation, out by strategy rule 2: what an application shows its user is not a protocol message, so no recording carries it.

Ignoring a notification is the absence of a reaction, which a trace cannot tell apart from the notification never mattering: a recording would have to carry a message the receiver sends because it did not ignore the notification, and the protocol defines none (answering a notification is forbidden anyway, BASE-011). The party that sent the invalid notification is judged instead, where it can be: CANC-018 for a cancellation naming a request its sender never issued in the session, CANC-019 for one naming `initialize`.
The trigger condition — the tool list actually changing — is server-internal state a recorded trace cannot evidence, so absence of the notification is never proof of violation.
How a client weighs annotations is internal trust policy with no wire footprint.

Input validation, access control, rate limiting, and output sanitization are server-internal enforcement without a deterministic wire signature. Of the four duties, mcp-everything-server implements and tests input validation (tests/roundtrip.rs: tool_call_with_missing_required_argument_is_a_protocol_error and neighbors); access control beyond the transport-layer Host/Origin gate, rate limiting, and output sanitization are not in its scope — it serves fixed synthetic fixtures to a loopback-only harness.
Name-comparison semantics are consumer-internal; tools.name-unique (TOOL-008) applies case-sensitive comparison in accordance with this clause.
Client-side validation has no wire footprint; the server-side half of the contract is TOOL-011's check.
A host application's approval UX is outside the protocol session; a trace shows invocations that happened, not the approvals that gated them.
Binds the application's user interface — what it shows, when it asks, whether a person is there. None of it is a message, and MCP deliberately does not mandate an interaction model.
Binds what the client hands to a language model, which is downstream of the session entirely.
Five client-side practices — confirmation prompts, showing inputs, validating results, timeouts, audit logs. Each happens inside the client or in its UI; none is a message.
The trigger condition — the resource list actually changing — is server-internal state a recorded trace cannot evidence.
Whether the client can fetch a URI on its own is a property of the client's environment, not of the recorded session.

URI validation is server-internal enforcement; a trace shows the URIs exchanged, not whether the server vetted them. mcp-everything-server's read path is fail-closed — unknown or malformed URIs resolve to None — asserted by template_rejects_malformed_instantiations (src/resources.rs) and the unknown-URI protocol-error assertion in resources_surface_matches_the_scenarios (tests/roundtrip.rs).
The premise — whether the client could fetch the URI directly — is a property of the client's environment, not of the session (the RES-003 argument).
Whether a failure case actually occurred (the resource was absent, an internal fault happened) is server-side ground truth a trace does not carry.
Which resources are sensitive and what controls guard them is deployment policy with no per-session observable.
Permission checks are server-internal enforcement; a trace shows the operations served, not the checks that admitted them.
The trigger condition — the prompt list actually changing — is server-internal state a recorded trace cannot evidence.
Validation thoroughness is implementation-internal; a trace shows the prompt traffic, not the vetting applied to it.
Whether a failure case actually occurred (the name was invalid, an argument was missing) is server-side ground truth a trace does not carry.
Client-side pagination handling is internal; a session whose lists fit one page exercises nothing.
Mechanized at the protocol level by LIFE-009's negotiated-capabilities-only check; this restatement adds no separately observable conduct.

Deciding whether free-form log data contains secrets or PII is semantic content analysis, not structural validation; offline heuristics would produce unsound, unfalsifiable verdicts — a fixed pattern list is deterministic but proves nothing about what it misses.
Whether a failure case actually occurred (the level was invalid for this server, configuration failed) is server-side ground truth a trace does not carry.
Rate policy, context relevance, naming consistency, and redaction are semantic internals (the LOG-002 argument).
Rate limiting, validation, access control, and monitoring are implementation-internal enforcement without trace-level observables.
Input validation, rate limiting, and access control are implementation-internal enforcement without a deterministic wire signature.
Whether a failure case actually occurred is server-side ground truth a trace does not carry.
Relevance ordering, fuzziness, rate policy, and input vetting are semantic internals without trace-level observables.
Debouncing and caching are client-internal and timing-shaped; checks may not consult time (determinism rule).
What a client assumes is internal state; the assumption has no wire footprint (MCP pagination requests carry no size parameter to inspect).
Cursor stability is cross-request server behavior over hidden state; gracefulness on invalid cursors requires knowing a cursor was invalid (the PAGE-003 argument).
How a client interprets a missing cursor, and what flows it supports, is client-internal; the wire-visible cursor discipline is PAGE-002's check.

Whether a requested field is "sensitive information" — the page's own definition is "secrets and credentials that grant access or authorize transactions" — is a judgement about meaning, not syntax: a schema property named `token` may be a display preference and one named `answer` may collect a password. A check would have to guess from field names, and a guess convicts conforming servers. The server's author decides it; nothing in the message settles it.

The counterpart of the form mode prohibition, and blocked by the same judgement: that an interaction "involves such sensitive information" is a fact about what the user will be asked for, which no message states, so a form mode request cannot be shown to have needed URL mode.

Binds the client's user interface — what it shows the user, offers them, or lets them do — and none of that reaches the wire: a recording carries the client's messages, not its screens. The reference host this project ships has no interactive interface at all (it answers from its interaction script, `crates/mcp-reference-host/src/handler.rs`), so the clause is a host-implementation property, reviewed in the host, never judged from a trace.

No declaration can violate it on the wire. The page makes an `elicitation` object naming neither mode "equivalent to declaring support for `form` mode only", so every declared `elicitation` capability names at least one mode. What remains is whether the client can actually handle the mode it declared, which is internal: a client that cannot still returns a well-formed `decline` or `cancel`.

A reading, not an act, like MRTR-007: a client's answers to a form mode request and to one without `mode` are the same messages (`accept` with `content`, `decline`, `cancel`), and `content` is optional in the result, so no answer shows which reading the client took. The server half — that such a request is form mode — is what `elicitation.mode-supported` and `elicitation.form-schema-present` apply.
UI behaviour: pre-populating a form is what the user sees before submitting. The submitted `content` cannot show it — the user may change or clear every default — so no message carries the clause.

Which client initiated an elicitation is a fact across connections, and a recording holds one session. A completion sent to the wrong client appears in that client's recording as a notification for an id its session never established — the observation `elicitation.complete-notification-id` judges under the clause that names the id, because the one recording cannot say which of the two rules was broken.
Ignoring leaves no trace: a client that ignored a notification for an unknown or completed id and one that acted on it internally send the same messages afterwards.
UI behaviour: the controls the client offers its user. The wire shows only whether a retry or cancellation was eventually sent, which a user may decline to do whatever controls exist.
Its condition — that URL mode elicitation is required before the request can proceed — is the server's own determination, which no message states; a `-32042` cannot be shown to be unwarranted.

Its antecedent — that a request cannot be processed until an elicitation completes — is the server's determination, and the page lets it ask by other means (it "MAY return" the error, or may send the elicitation while the request is pending). A server that chose another way sends no error, and nothing in the trace says it should have.

Server-internal state handling. How a server stores per-user state, protects it and binds it to an identity happens behind its own storage and authorization, and the identity it binds to is established outside the session's messages, by MCP authorization (whose pages this registry keeps out of scope, `sources.json`). Verified, where verified at all, by the server's own security review and tests; at `2026-07-28` the state a client carries is `requestState`, opaque by construction (MRTR-008).

Concerns what the server treats as authorization of its own users — an internal decision. A URL mode elicitation used to sign a user in to the server looks on the wire exactly like one used for a third-party grant; the difference is what the server does with the outcome.

Third-party credentials are opaque strings whose provenance no message declares: a check cannot tell one in a result from any other string, and by design they never enter the session at all. The obligation is the server's — credentials could only transit the client if the server sent them — and it is kept by the flow the server builds, outside the recording.

Token passthrough happens between the server and the third-party service, outside the MCP session; the recording holds only the client–server exchange, in which the client's credentials appear (as HTTP authorization) whether or not the server reuses them elsewhere.

By the clause's own words the interaction "happens outside the MCP protocol, without involving the MCP client": it is between the user's browser and the server or a third-party authorization server, so a recording of the MCP session cannot contain it.

The same barrier as the transit clause: a credential obtained through URL mode elicitation is an opaque string whose provenance no message declares, so a check cannot tell one in a result from any other value the server returns.
Binding is server-internal state, and the identity it binds to is established by authorization outside the session's messages, so no message shows whether an elicitation was bound to it.

The page's own examples put an `elicitationId` in the query, which is exactly the kind of value a pattern would misread.

Whether a URL grants access without further authentication is a property of the server it points to, observable only by dereferencing it — which a validator must not do (the client rules on the same page forbid even pre-fetching it), and which a recording does not contain.

Intent: the clause forbids URLs "intended to be clickable", and a form's `message` or a field's description may mention a URL for reference. A check for URL-shaped text would convict a server for mentioning a link, and the intent itself is not on the wire.

Its antecedent — that this is a non-development environment — is not in the trace. A loopback host suggests development without proving it, and a staging or internal host proves nothing either way, so an `http` URL is not by itself evidence of a violation. The scheme is recorded; the environment is not.

Policy and UI: whether a human reviews sampling requests, and whether they can deny one, is the client application's design. A request answered with a result may have been approved by a person or by policy; nothing in the answer says which.

The precondition half of the sentence. A client that has not declared `sampling.tools` does nothing wrong by receiving a tool-enabled request — the server does, and the sentence's other half (`sampling.tools-declared`) judges it. Nothing the client sends can break this half: the declaration is either made or not, and its absence becomes a violation only when such a request arrives, which is the server's act.

The Protected Resource Metadata document is not on the MCP endpoint, and a recording cannot show it. The `resource_metadata` URL names the server's own address, which `mcp-trace-capture` does not rewrite, so a client fetches the document past the proxy; the well-known fallback is built from the proxy's origin, and the proxy maps every path under the upstream's (`/.well-known/...` reaches `/mcp/.well-known/...`), where no server serves it. Where a fetch does pass through, its `http` event records no request target, so its JSON body cannot be told from any other.
